To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The level of IAA in the stem of Scots pine trees increased steadily during the period of cambial re‐activation and remained constant thereafter.
the level of IAA (indole‐3‐ acetic acid) increased steadily from the start of cambium reactivation, and that the concentration of IBA (indole‐butyric acid) was high in the dormant cambium.
The level of endogenous indol-3-acetic-acid (IAA) increases in the cambial stem region of large Scots pine trees during the period of active growth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the cambial activity and the concentration of indole- 3-acetic acid in the cambial regions of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestrs) stem.
the role of auxin (IAA) as the primary plant growth regulator in the control of the cambial activity and the seasonal pattern of xylem differentiation in the main stem of Pinus.
the role of the cambium in the regulation of the growth and form of the shoot and the stem of woody plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IAA is a growth regulator, but it is only one among many.
the level of endo‐genous IAA in the stem of P. sylvestris does not change in a simple and direct way in response to the changes in the level of cambial activity during the annual growth cycle.
IAA does not play a major role in regulating the seasonal variation in cambial activity of Pinus sylvester.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cambial region of Pinus sylvestris contains a pool of indole‐3 acetic acid (IAAA) which is not in equilibrium with that in the rest of the stem.
there is a seasonal pattern in the level of IAA in the stem cambium of Scots pine, and that this pattern does not appear to be related to the seasonal pattern of cambial activity.
the level of endogeneous IAA in the stem of P. sylvestris does not fluctuate in phase with the cambial activity, but that there are seasonal changes in the concentration of IIA in the cambial zone.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the seasonal variation of IAA in the stem of Scots pine is not simply a reflection of cambial activity, but is also related to other factors such as tree age, tree size and the developmental status of the cambium.
the seasonal variation of IAA in the pine stem is similar to that of the cambium, which suggests that it is a factor in regulating the cambial activity.
the cambial activity in Scots pine stems is not controlled by a simple fluctuation in endogenous IAA.
